extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in combinatorics / combinatorial design theory (readers of Proofs from THE BOOK)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria, definitions, and constructive methods for deciding when a partial Latin square can be completed to a full Latin square (Evans conjecture and Smetaniuk's constructive proof). Includes lemmas (Hall-theorem applications), conjugacy principles, and the explicit inductive completion algorithm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Latin square of order n
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain a Latin square, one has to fill the n^2 cells of an (n × n)-square array with the numbers 1, 2, . . ., n so that every number appears exactly once in every row and in every column.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent viewpoint: rows and columns each represent permutations of {1,...,n}. The line-array view (3 × n^2 array with lines R, C, E) is useful: the condition is that in any two lines all n^2 ordered pairs appear exactly once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Partial Latin square
rubrics_metrics.description: A partial Latin square of order n if some cells of an (n × n)-array are filled with numbers from the set {1, . . ., n} such that every number appears at most once in every row and column.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Necessary feasibility condition for any completion problem: initially any element appears at most once per row and column. The question studied: when can such a partial Latin square be completed to a Latin square of the same order?

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: (r × n)-Latin rectangle
rubrics_metrics.description: If a partial Latin square is of the form that the first r rows are completely filled and the remaining cells are empty, then we speak of an (r × n)-Latin rectangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An (r×n)-Latin rectangle is a partial configuration that admits extension-criteria via Hall's theorem; key base configuration in inductive completion arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugacy principle for partial Latin squares
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no special role for the elements: we may permute the symbols in each line arbitrarily (permutations of rows, columns or elements) and we may permute the three lines (R, C, E) of the line-array. Any conjugate of a partial Latin square is again a partial Latin square and a partial Latin square can be completed iff any conjugate can be completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical use in proofs: one may rearrange rows/columns/elements to place filled cells in convenient positions (e.g., top rows or below the diagonal) without changing completability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 1: Extendability of Latin rectangles (Hall's theorem application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any (r × n)-Latin rectangle, r < n, can be extended to an ((r+1)×n)-Latin rectangle and hence can be completed to a Latin square.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof method: For each column j let A_j be the set of numbers not appearing in column j; an admissible (r+1)-st row is a system of distinct representatives (SDR) for A_1,...,A_n. Use Hall's condition (H): each A_j has size n−r and every element appears in exactly n−r of the A_j, so any m of the sets contain at least m different elements, satisfying (H).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 2: Completion when at most n−1 cells are filled and bounded distinct-elements condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Let P be a partial Latin square of order n with at most n −1 cells filled and at most n^2 distinct elements, then P can be completed to a Latin square of order n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy (constructive): by conjugacy assume filled entries occupy the top r rows; order rows so f1 ≥ f2 ≥ ... ≥ fr and complete rows 1..r step-by-step until reaching an (r × n)-rectangle, then apply Lemma 1. The delicate step is completing a given row ℓ using Hall's theorem on sets A_j of elements not appearing in column j restricted to X (elements missing from row ℓ). Key inequalities used: (1) n − f_ℓ − ℓ + 1 > (ℓ − 1) + f_{ℓ+1} + ... + f_r and (2) m(n − f_ℓ − ℓ + 2 − m) > f_{ℓ+1} + ... + f_r for ranges of m; these guarantee Hall's condition for the relevant family A_j. (The text shows how to bound sizes of unions B of m sets and conclude |B| ≥ m.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Evans conjecture / Smetaniuk's theorem (main criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any partial Latin square of order n with at most n −1 filled cells can be completed to a Latin square of the same order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive inductive proof outline: use Lemma 2 to reduce to the case with more than n/2 distinct elements to locate an element appearing exactly once; permute rows/columns (using conjugacy) so that all filled cells lie below the diagonal except that single occurrence which lies on the diagonal. Remove that diagonal entry and delete the first row and last column to reduce to a partial Latin square of order n−1 with at most n−2 filled cells; complete by induction. Then perform a sequence of operations for k = 2..n−1: put n into cell (k,n) and exchange the diagonal entry x_k with that n, resolving collisions by a finite sequence of row-wise exchanges governed by a bipartite graph G_k; this process terminates and results in a full completion. Finally place n on diagonal and complete first row by missing elements of columns (Lemma 1). To recover the original arrangement, reverse the initial permutations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exchange procedure and termination criterion (graph/G_k argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: When inserting n into column n and exchanging it with diagonal entries x_k, if x_k already appears in the last column, perform row-wise exchanges propagating along entries; model these possible exchanges by a bipartite graph G_k whose vertices correspond to cells (i,k) and (j,n) and edges represent same-row or equal-entry relationships. All vertices have degree 1 or 2; the (k,n) vertex has degree 1 and initiates a finite path that ends at a value not present in column n, ensuring termination of the exchange chain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combinatorial-graph viewpoint guarantees no infinite loops during the exchange procedure and preserves Latin conditions (no duplicate entries in any row/column) throughout the exchanges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterexample / anti-pattern: n filled cells may prevent completion
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist partial Latin squares with only n cells filled (one per row or in particular placements) that cannot be completed — the text displays a margin example of a partial square with only n filled cells that clearly cannot be completed because of an unavoidable conflict in the upper-right corner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: the threshold 'at most n − 1 filled cells' in Evans' statement is sharp: having n filled cells does not guarantee completability; the placement of filled cells matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness in the final stage of Smetaniuk's construction
rubrics_metrics.description: After the exchange operations up to k = n−1 and placing n in (n,n), the first row can be completed uniquely by the missing elements of the respective columns, and reversing permutations yields an explicit completion of the original partial Latin square.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although intermediate steps may have choices, the described algorithm culminates in a uniquely determined completion of the modified configuration; reversing permutations gives a concrete completion of the original instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Hall's theorem / system of distinct representatives (general criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many completion steps reduce to finding a system of distinct representatives for a family of sets A_j (elements missing from column j, restricted to those missing from a target row). Hall's condition (for every subcollection the union has size at least the number of sets) is the decisive criterion to guarantee an admissible row (or extension) exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical recipe: define A_j appropriately for the targeted extension, estimate sizes and multiplicities (counting appearances above and below the row), and verify Hall's condition via combinatorial inequalities (as in the proofs of Lemma 1 and Lemma 2).
